cells.tense: You are at the point where the work has gotten specific and you know it.
cells.ask: Pick the next pass on it and do only that pass today, then see what the doing tells you the following one is.
cells.core: You're past the part where the work was a phase; it's a direction you picked and keep picking, one sitting at a time. The confidence sits in the return, not in any single good day. Another route could pull you off this one, but a wider range would come out of this bench rather than replace it. The choice doesn't need to be dramatic, but it does need to get made again; that's where the balance is kept. So make the next pass, one round only, and let its result name the round after. You'll feel the direction hold, and you'll have a way to keep holding it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep choosing this, and that's the thing holding.
cells.verb: going deep in one practice, one pass at a time
cells.place: a workbench, where the next move gets chosen

cells.tense: You will be bracing for a future depth the bench can't get to this week.
cells.ask: Do one pass at this week's pace, badly, then tell someone what the pass showed you.
cells.core: You're building for the version that finally arrives, and the bench doesn't get there on the timetable you've set. Every sitting becomes a test of whether it measures up, and the measuring eats the sitting. That's what turns a practice into a weight — the work itself is fine, but it's loaded with a future it hasn't earned yet. The pressure will reach a place where you're specializing so far ahead that the ordinary pass stops counting. Sharpen that. Go one pass at this week's pace, make it rough, then give it a voice — say what the pass showed to someone who will ask a plain question about it. The look of it can be loose; let the rough take its own standing.
cells.sheetLine: You're practicing for a future instead of in this one.
cells.verb: going deep in one practice, one pass at a time
cells.place: a workbench, where the next move gets chosen

cells.tense: There is a doorway you were walking toward, and you have stopped short of it.
cells.ask: Put one clean frame around the work you can finish this evening and send it to one person who will use it.
cells.core: The machinery is still there and the deliveries aren't. The work is on the bench, the sequence is known, and the forward motion isn't moving. It isn't the craft that left; it's that the same pass doesn't get taken, so the next one has no way of showing up. The structure out front has gone slack, and you feel it when someone asks what you're doing next. The fix isn't more effort into the gap; it's pushing one finished piece out into the open. Wrap the one you can wrap tonight, show it to someone who will use it, and let their use give it an edge. The direction will feel like something you can say again when it's moving.
cells.sheetLine: The bench is set, but the piece isn't going out.

cells.tense: You are already steering this practice and you talk about it like background noise.
cells.ask: Name this practice as one you chose, say it once out loud, then build the next sitting from what you actually want out of it.
cells.core: The work is running under your hands and you don't credit yourself for picking it. You call the hours a routine, the standard of the output the craft's own mood, the persistence something that just happens — but someone is deciding those sessions exist, and the decision is one you make at the bench. It's the same direction you keep picking; the fact of the decision and what you call it have come apart. The fix is small. Take one sitting where the work clearly moved, say out loud that you chose it, then build the next sitting from what you want back from the doing rather than from what the bench seems to ask. Nothing else needs rebuilding; owning it is what's missing.
cells.sheetLine: You're already at the bench, you just won't admit you chose it.

A reader could reasonably say the craft is going fine and the specialization just isn't the whole self, so the card's completion stays adjacent, not asserted as what they have already reached. Same ask, less setup, serves the writer and not the person; cut it.
